questions.question: Explain what aerial photographs are and why they are useful.
questions.expected_answer: Aerial photographs are photographs of the earth's surface taken from above by aircraft, helicopters, drones or balloons, usually a few hundred metres to a few kilometres up, so they show more detail of smaller areas than satellite images taken from space by sensors. Town planners use them to see urban growth and plan roads and housing, farmers and agricultural officers to monitor crops and erosion, engineers to plan roads, railways and dams, environmental scientists to monitor wetlands, forests and coasts, and mapmakers to make and update maps; South Africa's national mapping organisation uses them to produce 1:10 000 orthophoto maps. Because they record the ground at one moment, dated photographs from different years show change over time, such as township growth or the loss of farmland. Drones now make aerial photography cheaper and very detailed.

questions.question: Compare oblique and vertical aerial photographs, giving the advantages and disadvantages of each.
questions.expected_answer: An oblique photograph is taken with the camera tilted; in a low oblique the horizon is not visible and in a high oblique it is. It shows the sides and tops of features, so they are easy to recognise and heights can be seen, but the scale changes from large in the foreground to small in the background, tall features hide what is behind them and it cannot be used to measure accurately. A vertical photograph is taken with the camera pointing straight down and looks like a map, showing only roofs, treetops, roads and fields with no horizon; its scale is nearly constant, so distances and areas can be measured and it can be compared with a map, and nothing is hidden, but features are harder to recognise from directly above. Corrected vertical photographs with exactly constant scale are orthophotographs, used in orthophoto maps. Oblique is better for recognising features; vertical is better for measuring and mapping.

questions.question: Explain how natural and constructed features are identified on aerial photographs, and calculate the scale of a vertical photograph taken with a 152 mm lens from 1 520 m.
questions.expected_answer: Natural features, such as mountains, rivers, wetlands, beaches, dunes and natural forest, are formed by nature; constructed features, such as buildings, roads, railways, dams, harbours, fields and plantations, are made by people. Interpretation clues include tone (deep water dark, sand and concrete light), texture (smooth water or roads, rough forest), shape (regular straight lines and rectangles for constructed features, irregular curves for natural ones, such as a meandering river compared with a straight canal), size, shadow showing height and side profile, pattern (regular rows of houses or orchards, irregular informal settlements) and association with surroundings; several clues should be used together. Scale equals focal length divided by flying height in the same units: 0.152 m divided by 1 520 m equals 1/10 000, so the scale is 1:10 000 and 1 cm represents 100 m.
